strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea: constructing a geometry-grounded analog of byte-pair encoding for protein backbones, addressing genuine limitations of fixed-size, non-interpretable VQ-VAE codebooks used by prior PSTs (e.g., ESM3, ProToken, FoldSeek).

Rigorous mathematical formalization of backbone geometry (bond-residue motifs, entry/exit SE(3) frames, glue transforms) and a principled treatment of quantization drift correction via differentiable inverse kinematics with an end-frame loss.

Extensive and multi-faceted empirical evaluation: compression/distortion Pareto analysis, OOD generalization (CAMEO/CASP14), data efficiency (1% of pretraining data), token utilization/perplexity, a novel SSLM-Eval protocol for generative efficiency, and downstream transfer across 12 tasks/24 splits.

Strong quantitative results relative to VQ-VAE and continuous baselines on compression (0.27-0.36x BPR of ProToken), OOD generalization (1.16-1.28x vs 6.4x for VQ-VAE), and average downstream metrics (+15-43% relative gains over ESM3).

Interpretability contributions are compelling: near-perfect domain/segment agreement with CATH FunFam boundaries and qualitative expert case studies linking discovered motifs to known functional elements (binding pockets, transport motifs, phospho-recognition sites).

Thorough ablations (glue optimization necessity, Mmax saturation, multi-resolution behavior, task-specific vs task-agnostic tokenizer) and a detailed computational complexity analysis with practical mitigation strategies.
Substantial reproducibility effort: extensive appendices with full algorithmic pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, and dataset/preprocessing details.
weaknesses: The generative quality in absolute terms remains weak (scTM ~0.27, designability only 3-4%), which undercuts the claim that GEOBPE 'supports unconditional backbone generation' in a practically meaningful sense; comparisons to VQ-VAE baselines (which are also very low, ~1%) may reflect that the small-scale LM proof-of-concept is not yet convincing for either method.

Downstream transfer results are mixed rather than uniformly positive: several splits show GEOBPE underperforming ESM3 or other baselines (e.g., Rep -24%, Homo(Fold) -21%, CatInt(SupFam) -1.3%, FlexRMSF -8%), which is somewhat obscured by reporting only averages in the abstract/main claims.

The method involves many interacting heuristic components (k-medoids clustering, adaptive re-quantization, periodic global glue optimization, numerous hyperparameters such as bins, num_p, Mmax, glue_opt_every) without strong theoretical guarantees on convergence or optimality of the merge process, raising concerns about sensitivity and generalizability of default settings across datasets.

The ablation showing that GEOBPE trained on only 1% of data or with task-specific data yields no improvement is framed positively as 'data efficiency,' but could equally indicate limited representational capacity or a saturation/underfitting issue with the vocabulary construction, which is not fully explored.

Baseline comparisons may not be fully apples-to-apples given large differences in training data size and the use of pretrained ESM3 features as the backbone extractor for GEOBPE's downstream features (while VQ-VAE features are end-to-end learned), complicating attribution of performance gains to the tokenizer itself versus the feature extractor.

The interpretability evaluation relies substantially on a small number of qualitative, apparently LLM/expert-narrated case studies (3 proteins) with fairly subjective claims (e.g., 'suggests potential compatibility with membrane proteins'), which is not a rigorous or statistically grounded assessment of interpretability.

The CATH FunFam agreement metric is evaluated against a very weak random-segmentation baseline, which may inflate the apparent superiority of GEOBPE's segmentation without contextualizing against more competitive domain-segmentation baselines.
The method currently ignores side-chain geometry and sequence information entirely, limiting its immediate applicability to full multimodal protein modeling as motivated in the introduction.

The paper is very dense with heavy notation and 20+ algorithms relegated to appendices, which, despite aiding reproducibility, significantly hinders readability and may hamper independent verification and adoption by the community.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated method: the first geometry-grounded analog of byte-pair encoding for protein backbones, directly addressing known limitations of VQ-VAE-based protein structure tokenizers (fixed token size, codebook collapse, lack of interpretability, no multi-scale structure).

Rigorous geometric formalism (bond-residue notation, motif/glue definitions, SE(3) entry/exit frames) grounding the algorithm, with a principled treatment of quantization drift via differentiable inverse kinematics and end-frame loss.

Strong, broad empirical evaluation: compression-distortion Pareto analysis against ESM3, ProToken, VQ-VAE/AminoASeed baselines; OOD generalization (CAMEO/CASP14); 12 downstream tasks/24 splits; token efficiency and generative (SSLM) evaluation; and scaling studies up to 550K structures.

Interpretability contributions are compelling and differentiate the method from prior tokenizers: near-perfect agreement with CATH FunFam domain boundaries, secondary structure agreement analysis, and detailed expert case studies (SLC25A20, 14-3-3:Tau) linking discovered motifs to known functional/biochemical roles.

Extensive ablation studies (hyperparameter sensitivity for num_p, bins, glue_opt frequency, wR/wt, free_bonds, Mmax) and a formalized set of tokenizer 'principles' (Pareto-optimality, OOD generalization, downstream transfer) used to structure the evaluation.
Good reproducibility effort: code availability statement, detailed hyperparameter tables and guidelines, computational complexity analysis, and thorough appendix documentation of all algorithms.
weaknesses: The method is highly intricate (25+ algorithms, many interacting hyperparameters, multi-stage pipeline with clustering, quantization, and periodic global IK refinement), which raises concerns about practical reproducibility and accessibility despite the detailed documentation.

The headline claim of 'consistently outperforming leading PSTs across 12 tasks' is somewhat overstated: Table 1 shows continuous PSTs (ProteinMPNN, MIF) frequently outperform GEOBPE-TRANSFER (e.g., Rep, Homo-Fold, several flexibility tasks), so the comparison is favorable mainly against discrete/VQ-VAE baselines, not universally against all PST types.

The generative language modeling results (SSLM-Eval) use very small models (7.3M and 65.9M parameters) that the authors themselves acknowledge are 'not competitive with state-of-the-art backbone design models,' making the generative claims largely preliminary/qualitative rather than establishing practical utility.

Scalability evidence (550K AlphaFold DB structures) is only ~10x larger than the pretraining set and far short of ESM3-scale (236M structures) that the paper repeatedly references as the target regime for structure-native PLMs; worst-case complexity analysis shows O(N^2) terms that could become problematic at that scale.

Some interpretability results rely on comparisons against relatively weak baselines (e.g., random equal-length segmentations for CATH FunFam agreement), which may inflate the apparent significance of the reported near-perfect recall/F1/IOU numbers without stronger structurally-informed baselines (e.g., existing structural alphabets).

Downstream transfer ablations (Table 3, 4) reveal that GEOBPE vocabularies are largely insensitive to training data amount/task-specificity, which the authors interpret positively, but could also indicate limited representational flexibility/capacity of the learned vocabulary.
The paper is unusually long (48 pages including appendix) with most core evidentiary results relegated to appendices, making it harder to assess robustness of central claims from the main text alone.

strengths: A genuinely novel formulation: adapting the BPE merge-and-vocabulary paradigm to continuous SE(3) backbone geometry via k-medoids clustering of Geo-Pairs plus differentiable inverse-kinematics 'glue' correction to control drift accumulation is a creative and non-trivial technical contribution.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: compression/distortion Pareto analysis, OOD generalization on CAMEO/CASP14, data efficiency ablations, 12 downstream tasks across 24 splits, token efficiency/perplexity, a small-scale language-modeling study (SSLM-Eval), and a 10x data/model scaling study.

Strong headline results relative to VQ-VAE-style discrete tokenizers (FoldSeek, ESM3, VanillaVQ, AminoASeed): large bits-per-residue reductions, far better OOD test/train distortion ratios, and generally higher downstream transfer scores among discrete PSTs.

Genuine interpretability contribution: near-perfect recall of CATH FunFam domain boundaries, secondary-structure agreement analysis, and detailed expert case studies (SLC25A20, 14-3-3:Tau) linking discovered motifs to known functional sites.
Exceptionally thorough reproducibility documentation: detailed algorithmic pseudocode, computational complexity analysis, and an extensive hyperparameter guide with sensitivity studies.
weaknesses: The abstract/intro claim of 'consistently outperforming leading PSTs across 12 tasks' is overstated: Table 1 shows continuous PSTs (ProteinMPNN, MIF) frequently beat GEOBPE-TRANSFER (e.g., Rep, BindInt-Fold-adjacent tasks, FlexRMSF, several Homo/CatInt splits), and GEOBPE-TRANSFER even underperforms other discrete PSTs on some splits (e.g., CatInt SupFam -1.3%, Homo-Fold -21.4%), so the comparison is best characterized as 'best among discrete PSTs on average' rather than a uniform win.

The method exposes a large number of task-specific hyperparameter settings (different num_p/bins configurations for compression vs. transfer vs. Pareto-front experiments, Section K.1), which raises concern that results are tuned per-benchmark rather than reflecting a single robust tokenizer configuration, undermining the 'architecture-agnostic, general-purpose tokenizer' narrative.

Generative quality via GEOBPE+SSLM is weak in absolute terms (scTM 0.2-0.4, designability 1-21%) and explicitly acknowledged as 'not competitive with state-of-the-art backbone design models,' limiting the practical significance of the language-modeling application beyond a relative tokenizer comparison.

Comparisons against ESM3 (0.016-0.021x BPR) are confounded by vastly different training data scale, model capacity, and architecture; framing this primarily as a 'tokenizer efficiency' win is questionable since ESM3's codebook is entangled with a much larger end-to-end system.

The method is algorithmically very complex (25 algorithms, many interacting components: quantizer estimation, k-medoids, priority dictionaries, batch/single-boundary glue optimization, periodic global refinement), which raises practical reproducibility and implementation-burden concerns despite the detailed appendix, and increases risk of subtle implementation-dependent behavior.

Expert case studies and functional interpretability claims (Section 6, App. H) are qualitative and somewhat anecdotal/subjective narrative rather than rigorously validated against a quantitative ground truth beyond the CATH FunFam recall/precision numbers.

Backbone-only scope (no side chains/sequence) and the analysis showing worse fidelity on smaller/less-packed folds (e.g., Mainly-Alpha bundles) indicate the method's strong performance may be somewhat structure-class dependent despite claims of general robustness.

The paper is extremely long and dense, with core methodological and evaluation content spread thinly across a 48-page document; this raises concerns about whether the marginal contribution over prior structural alphabets (de Brevern et al., Mackenzie) and VQ-based PSTs is as large as claimed once overclaiming and cherry-picked settings are discounted.

strengths: Genuine methodological novelty: GeoBPE is the first BPE-style analog for continuous protein backbone geometry, combining k-medoids clustering of Geo-Pairs with differentiable inverse-kinematics-based glue-angle correction to control drift — a principled solution to a real gap (fixed-size, non-interpretable VQ-VAE codebooks) in protein structure tokenization.

Strong and multi-faceted empirical validation: the paper reports large compression gains (0.27-0.36x BPR of ProToken), excellent OOD generalization (test/train RMSD ratio ~1.1-1.3 vs 6.4x for VQ-VAE baselines), and strong downstream transfer across 12 tasks/24 splits, with consistent wins over multiple competitive discrete and continuous PST baselines.

Extensive and rigorous ablation and sensitivity analysis (Appendix A, K.3) covering data efficiency (1% training data), Mmax saturation, glue-optimization frequency, bin/num_p sensitivity, and rigid-body refinement necessity, which substantially strengthens confidence in the claimed properties.

Interpretability is empirically grounded, not just anecdotal: near-perfect agreement with CATH FunFam domain boundaries (F1≈0.996), secondary-structure agreement analysis, and multiple detailed expert case studies (SLC25A20, 14-3-3:Tau) connecting discovered motifs to known biochemical function.

High reproducibility effort: exhaustive algorithmic pseudocode (25 algorithms), computational complexity analysis, hyperparameter documentation with practical guidelines, and a scaling study to 550K structures and 10x larger models showing the approach is practically extensible.
weaknesses: The method is extremely complex with many interacting hyperparameters (num_p, bins, glue_opt_every, Mmax, wR/wt, etc.) across different use cases (compression vs. representation vs. LM); despite the detailed appendix guidance, this raises real concerns about ease of adoption and out-of-the-box reproducibility by other groups.

Downstream transfer results are mixed in places (e.g., GEOBPE-TRANSFER underperforms on Rep, some CatInt/Homo splits, FlexRMSF), and the paper's narrative sometimes emphasizes average gains while downplaying these regressions, which is only partially addressed in the discussion.

Comparisons across the SSLM-Eval generative benchmark and downstream transfer are potentially not on fully equal footing (VQ-VAE baselines trained end-to-end with joint feature/codebook learning vs. GeoBPE-Transfer leveraging a large pretrained ESM3 feature extractor Θ), making it harder to isolate the tokenizer's own contribution from that of the underlying feature extractor.

Absolute generative quality remains weak (scTM ~0.27-0.41, designability up to 21% even with 10x data/params) and the paper itself acknowledges it is not competitive with SOTA backbone design models, so the generative-modeling contribution is more a proof-of-concept than a demonstrated capability.

The method currently omits side chains/sequence entirely, and computational complexity analysis shows worst-case O(N^2) / O(sum M_t^2) behavior that is only tamed via a heuristic Mmax cap, whose optimality is empirically observed but not theoretically justified.
